In particular, it requires $O(mk^2)$ steps, where $m$ is the number of times we form $B$.

issues.failure_explanation: Computing all eigenvalues of a dense symmetric k x k matrix costs O(k^3) (e.g., the QR algorithm; the cited Golub-Van Loan), not O(k^2). Each trial therefore costs O(k^3) (k^2 kernel evaluations plus the eigendecomposition), so the framework costs O(mk^3), not the advertised O(mk^2). The qualitative guarantee of subquadratic-in-n cost survives for k << n, but the stated rates are mathematically wrong.

failure_location.quote: This new framework requires $O(mk^2)$ computations, where $m$ is a constant that depends on the desired approximation accuracy.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace O(k^2) by O(k^3) for the eigenvalue computation and O(mk^2) by O(mk^3) for the framework; no other change is needed because the subquadratic-in-n conclusion is preserved.
issues.overall_effect: The advertised per-trial and total complexity (O(k^2), O(mk^2)) is incorrect; the subquadratic-in-n guarantee and all eigenvalue-quantile claims are unaffected.
issues.title: Eigenvalue-computation complexity misstated as O(k^2) (framework cost O(mk^2) instead of O(mk^3))
issues.why_classification: A one-token correction fixes the rates and the advertised subquadratic guarantee survives unchanged, so the repair is local and routine with no mathematical loss.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The sets $S=\{1,2,3,4,5,7,9,12,13,14,22,23,29,30,31\}$ (blue dots) and $T$ (solid red dashes), where $T$ is picked such that $\sum_{i=1}^{15}a_i^r/15=\sum_{i=1}^5b_i^r/5$ for $r=1,\ldots,5$. Hence, $T$ is approximately $\{1.51216,6.52312,9.54601,20.5897,30.1624\}$.
Proposition~\ref{prop:momentmatching} shows, for example, that $b_3\leq a_{10},a_{11},a_{12}\leq b_5$.

issues.failure_explanation: As printed, the proposition claims b_{ceil(jk/n)-1} <= a_j <= b_{ceil(jk/n)+1} with b_0=0, b_{k+1}=infty. For j=1 this says a_1 <= b_2, which is false in general: in the paper's own example (n=15, k=5), a_1=31 > 20.5897=b_2, and b_3=9.54601 > 7=a_{10}, contradicting the stated b_3 <= a_{10}. The correct interlacing is the reverse inequality, exactly as already written in eq:interlacing and Corollary cor:momentmatching (sigma_{ceil(jk/n)-1}(B) >= sigma_j(A) >= sigma_{ceil(jk/n)+1}(B) with sigma_0(B)=infty, sigma_{k+1}(B)=0), and it is the direction that follows from the proof's quoted CDF bounds 1-sum_{j>=i} lambda(x_j) <= F_S(x_i) <= sum_{j<=i} lambda(x_j) with lambda=1/k. The figure caption (fig:momentinterlace) also repeats the reversed inequality.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Reverse the two inequalities in the statement to b_{ceil(jk/n)-1} >= a_j >= b_{ceil(jk/n)+1} and swap the boundary conventions to b_0=infty, b_{k+1}=0; fix the figure caption to b_5 <= a_{10},a_{11},a_{12} <= b_3. This matches eq:interlacing, the corollary, and the proof, with no loss of content.
issues.overall_effect: The proposition is false as printed and its illustration shows the wrong direction; all downstream results (eq:interlacing, cor:momentmatching, the framework's quantile bounds) already use the correct direction, so no formal dependent is invalidated.
issues.title: Proposition prop:momentmatching states the interlacing in the false (reversed) direction, with swapped boundary conventions
issues.why_classification: The correction is a forced, local direction swap (dictated by eq:interlacing, the corollary, the proof's bounds, and the paper's own example); every substantive claim survives, so the repair is minor.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof asserts that matching moments for r=1,...,k implies mu_i = nu_i 'for each i in N', which is false: matching the first k moments of a k-point measure determines the higher moments of that measure but not of S (e.g., k=1, S={1,3}, T={2}: mu_1=nu_1=2 but mu_2=5 != 4=nu_2). Moreover the Christoffel-function argument needs moments up to order 2k-1: the determinants defining P_j and D_j involve mu_0,...,mu_{2j-1} (hence mu_{2k-1} for P_k), and the orthogonality sum_l c_{i,j,l} mu_l = delta_{i,j} for deg(P_iP_j) up to 2k needs mu_{2k}; the hypothesis provides only mu_1,...,mu_k. So the proof does not establish the proposition (even with the corrected inequality direction) from its stated hypotheses; the polynomials P_j are not even determined by the hypothesis.

failure_location.quote: our assumptions are equivalent to requiring that $\mu_i=\nu_i$ for each $i=1,\ldots,k$, and therefore for each $i\in\mathbb{N}$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Supply a proof of the interlacing using only the k matched moments (e.g., via degree-(k-1) Lagrange/quadrature test polynomials at the b_i), or strengthen the hypothesis to moment matching through order 2k-1 (which would also require strengthening the corollary and the trace-matching application).
issues.overall_effect: The proposition is unproven from its stated hypotheses; cor:momentmatching, whose proof applies the proposition, inherits the gap, and with it the theoretical basis of the framework's quantile bounds.
issues.title: Proof of prop:momentmatching uses moment matching to order 2k-1, which the hypothesis (k moments) does not provide
issues.why_classification: The corrected statement is very likely true, but the given proof cannot be patched locally; a contained yet genuinely new argument is needed, which is more than a routine fix but avoids reworking the paper's architecture.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The second inequality in Equation~\eqref{eq:approxexpect} follows from Equation~\eqref{eq:quickdecay} in a similar way.

issues.failure_explanation: (i) The condition demands the walk ratio to equal s+epsilon exactly for all s in [t,1]; at s=1 the ratio is identically 1, forcing epsilon=0, and the constant walk (|pi|=1) has ratio int_{[0,s]^l} kappa(x,x)^r / int_{[0,1]^l} kappa(x,x)^r, which for translation-invariant kernels (kappa(x,x) constant, as in all of the paper's examples) equals s, again forcing epsilon=0. So the hypothesis is unsatisfiable for any epsilon>0 and any translation-invariant kernel: the proposition is vacuous as stated. (ii) Even read as an approximate condition, the additive form yields the wrong conclusion: substituting the condition at s=1/z_1 and using E[z_1^{l-1}] = (k/n) binom(n,l)/binom(k,l) from eq:specialdistrib gives the exact normalized trace ratio 1 + epsilon * (W_l-weighted average of (n-l)/(k-l) over walk-types l), which exceeds 1+epsilon whenever epsilon>0 (e.g., the l=2 walks contribute the factor (n-2)/(k-2)); the lower bound 1-epsilon holds trivially since the ratio is >= 1. Hence the upper bound 1+epsilon in eq:approxexpect is false under the stated hypothesis; the correct condition is multiplicative, ratio = s(1 +/- epsilon), under which the same computation yields the stated two-sided bound exactly.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate eq:quickdecay as an approximate multiplicative condition, e.g., (1-epsilon) s <= ratio <= (1+epsilon) s for s in [t,1) (the constant walk's ratio is exactly s and must be exempted or absorbed); the proof's chain then yields eq:approxexpect with the stated two-sided bound.
issues.overall_effect: The main proposition's hypothesis is vacuous as stated (no translation-invariant kernel satisfies it with epsilon>0), and its two-sided relative-error conclusion is false even under an approximate reading (the true upper error is amplified by a factor up to about n/k); the theoretical guarantee behind the numerical examples is affected.
issues.title: Condition eq:quickdecay is misstated: unsatisfiable as written, and its additive form makes the upper bound in eq:approxexpect false
issues.why_classification: The defect is a misstated hypothesis (exact/additive instead of approximate/multiplicative, closed interval); once restated, the proof goes through unchanged and the advertised +/-epsilon guarantee survives, so the repair is a contained reoptimization of the premise rather than a new architecture.

issues.failure_explanation: The proposition is stated for all d in N and is applied for d=3 and d=6, but eq:quickdecay integrates over the 1-dimensional domains [0,s]^l and demands ratio s+epsilon, and the proof's change of variables uses F(x) = (1/Z_1,...,1/Z_k)·x, i.e., y_j = x_j/z_j, dropping the 1/d in the proposition's own definition y_j ~ (1/z_j)^{1/d} U[0,1]; the walk integrals are written over [0,1/z_1]^l with factor z_1^l instead of [0,z_1^{-1/d}]^{ld}. For d>=2, translation-invariant rapidly decaying kernels give walk ratios approximately s^d, not s (the backtrack walk x_1 -> x_2 -> x_1 gives int prod_i (s-|u_i|)_+ phi(u)^2 du / int phi^2 ≈ s^d, and the constant walk gives exactly s^d), so eq:quickdecay is unsatisfiable for d>=2 for the paper's entire kernel class. Thus the proposition provides no guarantee in the advertised moderate/high-dimensional regime, and the paper's d=3,6 examples fall outside the theorem as stated (empirically the framework works in 3D, where the stated condition fails).

failure_location.quote: Define $x_i\sim U[0,1]$ and $y_j\sim(1/z_j)^{1/d}U[0,1]$ for $1\leq i\leq n$ and $1\leq j\leq k$

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate the condition in d dimensions (ratio = s^d (1 +/- epsilon) over domains ([0,s]^d)^l, s in [t,1)) and adapt the proof's walk integrals to [0,z_1^{-1/d}]^{ld}; the chain then goes through, but the corrected condition must be re-verified for the example kernels (the source contains only the 1D limit argument).
issues.overall_effect: The proposition is vacuous for d >= 2: the central advertised regime (Euclidean space of any or moderate/high dimension, the paper's main advantage over banded and Nystrom methods) is excluded, and the d=3,6 numerical examples have no theoretical cover.
issues.title: The quick-decay hypothesis and its proof are one-dimensional, so the proposition is vacuous for d >= 2, the advertised high-dimensional regime
issues.why_classification: An advertised regime is excluded: as stated the theorem covers only d=1, and restoring the high-dimensional regime requires restating the central hypothesis and re-establishing it for the example kernels, which the source does not support; this is a major loss that a local patch cannot fix.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof's key inequality (the step from (1-epsilon) z_1^{l-1} int_{[0,1]^l} prod kappa to z_1^l int_{[0,1/z_1]^l} prod kappa) applies eq:quickdecay at s=1/z_1, but the condition is only assumed for s in [t,1]; the argument therefore requires z_1 in [1,1/t] for (almost) every z in the support of Xi. No such support constraint is assumed in the proposition, and Proposition prop:distributionexistence only guarantees nonnegative support; the natural solution Z=1/B with B ~ Beta(k,n-k) (whose moments match eq:specialdistrib) is unbounded above, and the example's atom at delta=130.90 forces t <= 1/130.9, incompatible with the correlation length 1/sqrt(1000) of the example kernel e^{-1000(x-y)^2}. For z_1 outside [1,1/t] the needed inequality is unjustified and can fail.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add the hypothesis that Xi is supported on [1,1/t] (or that eq:quickdecay holds for all s in (0,1]) and verify that a distribution satisfying the moment conditions of eq:specialdistrib exists with this support; this compatibility is not established in the source.
issues.overall_effect: The proof's central estimate is unestablished on the part of the support of Xi outside [1,1/t]; the proposition's guarantee does not follow for the constructed distributions, including the paper's own Example ex:samplingdistribution.
issues.title: Proof applies the quick-decay condition at s=1/z_1 without ensuring z in [1,1/t]; the support of Xi is unconstrained
issues.why_classification: An omitted hypothesis must be added and its compatibility with the moment problem verified (a contained but nontrivial addition, unresolved in the source); the conclusion survives under the added assumption, so the repair is moderate rather than serious.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof claims (1/((k/n) binom(n,k))) mu_l = <v_i,v_j>_V for i+j=l, where mu_l = ((k/n) binom(n,l+1))/binom(k,l) = (n-k)!(k-1-l)!/(n-1-l)!. With the stated weight x^{n-k-1}(1-x)^{k+1}, the Gram entry is (n-k) int_0^1 x^{n-k-1}(1-x)^{k-l} dx = (n-k)!(k-l)!/(n-l)!, which differs from the target by the factor (k-l)/(n-l) (for l=0 the factor is k/n). The identity holds with the weight x^{n-k-1}(1-x)^k (exponent k, not k+1), which is the single forced correction: then <v_i,v_j>_V = (n-k)!(k-1-l)!/(n-1-l)! = (1/((k/n) binom(n,k))) mu_l exactly, and similarly for the w_j and H'_{k,n}.
